title: Product Management for Engineers
description: How a software engineer should think about products: problem framing, discovery and delivery, prioritization, metrics and experiments, strategy, and what a product manager actually needs to know and do.

generator.request: I want study material on product management: how a product engineer should think, what exactly one product manager should know, and a course on that. I am an engineer, but I want to learn how to think from a product perspective as well.

modules.title: Discovery vs Delivery: The Four Product Risks and the Build-to-Learn Loop
modules.description: Why product work is risk reduction before it is building: the four risks, who owns each, which cheap test reduces which risk, and where practitioners disagree on how discovery should be done.
modules.scope: In: the mechanism that separates product work from delivery. Feature teams vs product teams (a roadmap of outputs vs a set of problems and outcomes); a feature as a hypothesis with a measured base rate of failure; the four risks (value, usability, feasibility, business viability) and why the original three-risk framing was revised; risk ownership in a trio; build-to-learn vs build-to-earn and the stated cost rule for discovery; which technique (interviews, prototypes, randomized experiments, shaping) reduces which risk and what each cannot tell you; the AI-era change in prototype cost. Out: framing the problem and understanding users (page 2), ranking and scheduling (page 3), experiment design and metrics (page 4), the role map and the PR/FAQ's mechanics (page 5), viability in depth (page 6). After reading, the reader can classify a proposed feature by the least-tested of the four risks, pick the cheapest technique that reduces it, and say what an engineer owns (feasibility) and what he is still accountable for noticing (the other three). Writer cautions: the 10-20% pay-off figure appears twice with different bases (S2: Bing/Google metric-improvement rate, sourced to Manzi 2012; S5: roadmap items with positive ROI, unnamed analysts) - state the bases separately and never merge them with the 1/3 (Microsoft), ~30% (Slack monetization) and '90% wrong' (Netflix, secondhand via Moran 2007) figures; 'at least one order of magnitude cheaper' and '3-5 iterations' are SVPG's own estimates (S5 and S6 are the same organization, not independent) - attribute, do not state as findings; S27 is not a grounding source (not fetched; only the 2008 first-edition table of contents is known) - the three-to-four-risk revision rests on S3 alone, attribute it to S3; S9 recommends a product outcome at the tree's root yet also says it starts with business value - note, do not resolve; S9's author discloses a commercial tie; weekly-interview cadence is prescription, not evidence; S6 is dated 2026-04-27 and its AI-role claims are likely to change within a year. Worked illustrations may use on-device inference scenarios but must be labeled hypothetical and carry no invented figures.
topics: Feature team vs product team: a roadmap of outputs vs a set of problems and desired outcomes, and what each team can be held accountable for (S5)

A feature is a hypothesis: base rates of success by domain - 1/3 at Microsoft, 10-20% in well-optimized domains, ~30% of Slack monetization experiments, '90% wrong' at Netflix (secondhand) - and what each figure actually measures (S2 Ch. 1 Tenet 3); SVPG's separately-based 10-20% of roadmap items (S5)
Derived arithmetic: expected builds per successful idea at 10-33% hit rates, and how much discovery spend per build the base rate can justify (derived from S2 and S5 figures, labeled as derived)

The four risks defined - value, usability, feasibility, business viability - the claim that value is usually hardest and viability most under-appreciated, and why the first-edition three-risk framing let business value slip (S3)
Risk ownership in a trio: PM for value and viability, designer for usability, lead engineer for feasibility; what the engineer is still expected to notice in the other three (S3, S9)

Build to learn vs build to earn: discovery's incentive is to determine quickly whether an idea works; prototypes made mostly by the product team; the stated cost rule and 3-5 iterations as SVPG's estimate (S5, S6)

Matching technique to risk: which of interviews, prototypes, randomized experiments, shaping and written vetting reduces which risk, at what relative cost, with what blind spot (S1, S2, S5, S6, S9, S16)

Continuous interviewing as a discovery cadence: weekly interviews, revisit the opportunity tree every three to four interviews, compare more than one solution per opportunity (S9), against PostHog's rule of thumb of one interview per week per PM (S20)
Randomized experiments as arbiter and their reach: a portfolio of near-optimization plus a few radical bets; what experiments cannot test; mechanics deferred to page 4 (S2 Ch. 1)
Shape-then-bet as discovery: shaped work is rough, solved and bounded before anyone bets; no customer-research cadence prescribed; ideas that matter come back (S1 Ch. 2, Ch. 7)
AI and discovery: a prototyping and decision-support role in discovery vs an automation and code-generation role in delivery; the 'constant, erratic change' caution (S6; flagged as likely to change)
disagreements: How should discovery be done: weekly interviews, prototypes, experiments, or shape-and-bet?

modules.title: From Request to Problem: Framing, Jobs-to-be-Done and Opportunity Trees
modules.description: How a feature request becomes a problem statement with a boundary, what jobs-to-be-done changes about understanding users compared with personas, and how an opportunity solution tree organizes what interviews turn up.
modules.scope: In: the step before any solution. Flipping from 'what could we build' to 'what is going wrong'; the problem as one specific story; 'good' as relative to constraints and the grab-bag red flag; reframing stakeholder requests; where problem inputs come from and how each channel distorts them; demographic personas vs jobs (the milkshake case); opportunity solution trees (outcome, opportunities, solutions, assumption tests); what a product-minded engineer does with a spec he is handed. Out: interview craft, survey design and usability testing (no fetched source; excluded), appetite and ranking (page 3), goals-signals-metrics and HEART (page 4), pitch and PRD formats (page 5). After reading, the reader can turn a request into a one-story problem statement with a boundary, state the job behind a user segment, and lay out an outcome-opportunity-solution tree with testable assumptions. Writer cautions: jobs-to-be-done is thinly covered. S10 is a secondhand HBS report of Christensen's teaching note (40% of milkshakes bought in the morning, the commute constraints) - cite it as one case, secondhand; S29 was not fetched and supports only what the book claims (jobs, not customers, drive innovation success), not the mechanism, and its publisher blurb is not evidence that the framework works; the rival JTBD school (Ulwick: a long boring commute is context, not the job) rests on a search snippet only - mark unverified; do not use the Mom Test rules (secondary summaries only) or the 2016 HBR article (paywalled, not fetched). The one-day-vs-six-week permissions example is Basecamp's own anecdote (S1) - attribute. S8 (2005) and S9 are prescriptive with no outcome data. Mark as unverified any application of jobs or opportunity trees to a developer-facing runtime (no source covers it). Illustrations from on-device inference are hypothetical and carry no invented figures.
topics: The framing flip: from 'What could we build?' to 'What's really going wrong?'; narrowing a problem until a six-week project becomes a one-day change (S1 Ch. 3, Basecamp's own example)
The problem as one specific story that shows why the status quo does not work, and why a story constrains better than a requirement list (S1 Ch. 6, ingredient 1)
'Good' is relative to constraints: no absolute best solution; grab-bag projects and the '2.0' label as framing failures (S1 Ch. 3)
Reframing requests: stakeholder-originated feature requests turned into problems, and the engineer who does not settle for a spec and jumps to implement it (S7, S23)
Where problems come from and how each channel distorts them: customer interviews, sales, support, stakeholders, the team's own usage; sales and support inputs arrive without context (S9, S7, S23)
Personas as design archetypes: user profiles, goals and tasks in a 2005 PRD, the 'Leon the Power Seller' example, and what a demographic profile leaves out (S8 Step 3)

Jobs-to-be-done: customers 'hire' a product for a job; the milkshake case (40% of milkshakes bought first thing in the morning by commuters; long boring commute, in a hurry, work clothes, at most one free hand); why demographics correlate with but do not cause purchase (S10); the book's claim that understanding jobs, not customers, drives innovation (S29, claim only)
What a 'job' is not agreed to be: the dispute over whether the commute is the job or its context (unverified; search snippet only)

Opportunity solution tree: outcome at the root, opportunities as customer needs, pain points and desires, solutions beneath, assumption tests; why compare more than one solution; garbage-in warning; no company-wide tree (S9)
The tension inside the opportunity tree: a product outcome at the root vs the page's own 'starts with business value' (S9)
Framing tests: the elevator-pitch test for a product's purpose and the requirement that objectives be prioritized and measurable (S8 Step 2)
Framing a developer-facing technical product: who 'the user' is when the customer is a developer integrating a runtime - a hypothetical application of jobs and the tree, marked unverified
disagreements: Personas or jobs-to-be-done for understanding users?

modules.title: What to Build and When: Appetite, Cost of Delay, Backlogs and Roadmaps
modules.description: How teams rank and schedule work - RICE, appetite-and-bet, cost of delay, backlog attrition, cycles and outcome roadmaps - and where the methods disagree about estimates, backlogs and dates.
modules.scope: In: ranking and scheduling mechanisms and what each optimizes. RICE with a derived worked example from S11's inputs; appetite vs estimate; Reinertsen's cost of delay and queue argument (Ch. 1 only) with the writer's own derived utilization-delay arithmetic flagged as derived; backlog attrition (Shape Up, Linear) against the Bing counter-case; six-week and two-week cycles and the betting table; the roadmap critique, outcome roadmaps and high-integrity date commitments. Out: finding which ideas are worth ranking (page 1), OKR grading and the OEC (page 4), who attends the betting table as a role question (page 5), opportunity sizing and business cases (excluded: no fetched source). After reading, the reader can choose a prioritization method for a given context, compute and stress-test a RICE ranking, state what a date commitment costs, and say what happens to an idea that is not ranked. Writer cautions: only the table of contents and Chapter 1 of Reinertsen (S28) were fetched - use the primary wording 'only 15 percent of product developers know the cost of delay associated with their projects' (Ch. 1 p. 4; his own course surveys of developers, not PMs) and never the secondary '85% of PMs' figure; the 50-to-1 spread is Ch. 1 footnote 1, p. 5; WSJF only as SAFe's page states it (relative cost of delay divided by relative job duration), its derivation (Ch. 2-9) is unfetched - mark unverified; the maxim 'if you only quantify one thing, quantify the Cost of Delay' is attributed on SAFe's page and not verified in the book. The RICE formula appears only as an image on S11's page and the page does not print scores for its worked example - the scores are derived arithmetic, say so; the observation that RICE confidence is not calibrated against base rates is the researcher's, not S11's or S2's - label it. The Bing figure (+12% revenue, over $100M/year in the US, six months in the backlog) is S2 Ch. 1 p. 3 only - attribute. S4's numbers are hypothetical illustrations; S1 and S17 carry no measured evidence. Queueing derivations are the writer's own and must be labeled as such.
topics: The standard roadmap and its critique: a prioritized list of features or projects that tells teams what to do; its command-and-control lineage (S4)

Outcome roadmaps: vision, prioritized business objectives per team, tell the team the problem not the solution; the hypothetical onboarding-time objective as illustration, not data (S4; OKR mechanics are on page 4)
High-integrity commitments: when a date is legitimate, the discovery work that must back it, its cost, and why dates are used sparingly (S4, S7)

RICE: Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort in person-months; the Impact scale (3, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25) and Confidence scale (100%, 80%, 50%, below 50% a moonshot); worked example with derived scores 675, 400 and 800 and a sensitivity check; limits - impact is a guess, dependencies unmodelled, confidence uncalibrated (S11 against S2)

Appetite vs estimate: a time budget set before the design, fixed time and variable scope, the small batch (one designer, one or two programmers, one to two weeks) vs the big batch, why over-specified work is harder to estimate (S1 Ch. 2-3)

Cost of delay: FIFO is rarely economically optimal in product development, different projects have different delay costs, only 15% of developers know theirs, answers vary 50 to 1 when not calculated; WSJF as SAFe states it (S28 Ch. 1)

Queues and utilization: why queues look free without a cost of delay, the reported 98.5% utilization and the 2% who measure queues; a derived delay-vs-utilization curve, labeled as the writer's derivation (S28 Ch. 1 pp. 6-7)
Backlog attrition: Shape Up's 'important ideas come back' and the grooming cost; Linear's 'important ones will resurface, low priority ones will never get fixed' (S1 Ch. 7, S17)

The counter-case: the Bing ad-headline change that sat six months in a backlog and was worth over $100M/year, against 10,000+ experiments a year and such wins only once every few years - what attrition costs and what a cheap test recovers (S2 Ch. 1 pp. 3, 5)

Cycles and the betting table: six-week cycle plus two-week cool-down, circuit breaker with no default extension, uninterrupted time, a betting call of an hour or two; against n-week cycles with two weeks most common and space reserved for unplanned work (S1 Ch. 7-8, S17, S18)
Planning horizons: no roadmap and no central list (S1), a roadmap of themes for about six months with projected end dates (S18), outcome objectives (S4) - what a 'date' means in each
Which method for which context: a decision table of input, what each method optimizes, failure mode, and strength of evidence
disagreements: Roadmaps and backlogs: reshape, abolish or keep?
Prioritization: estimate and rank, set an appetite and bet, or let attrition filter?

modules.title: Metrics, Experiments and Goals: OEC, Guardrails, HEART, OKRs and Trust
modules.description: How to define success for a product, test whether a change achieved it, set goals a team can be held to, and decide how much to trust the data - including for ML features that behave probabilistically.
modules.scope: In: the overall evaluation criterion, guardrails and the three organizational tenets; PULSE and HEART metrics, normalization and the seven-day-active trap; the Goals-Signals-Metrics process; what experiment base rates imply for a portfolio; Twyman's law; data-driven vs 70%-information judgment; OKR mechanics and the alternatives (OEC plus guardrails, initiatives, bets); the 18 human-AI interaction guidelines and the speed-vs-trust tension for adaptive features. Out: experiment statistics beyond Kohavi Ch. 1 (variance reduction, sample ratio mismatch, interference, long-term effects; Parts IV-V - excluded), product analytics instrumentation (funnels, cohorts), building an experimentation platform, offline-vs-online evaluation of ML models (the one candidate paper, the Booking.com KDD 2019 paper, could not be fetched - state this as a gap), strategy (page 6), roadmaps (page 3). After reading, the reader can write a goal-signal-metric chain for a feature, choose an OEC and guardrails for it, grade an OKR set, and state what evidence would justify shipping with or without an experiment. Writer cautions: for S2 only the front matter, table of contents, Preface and Chapter 1 were fetched - later-chapter references are table-of-contents pointers only; the success-rate figures are four different bases and must stay separate (the idea-attrition chart lives on page 1; here they serve the portfolio argument only); Apple under Jobs not testing ads is one quoted sentence in S2; the claim that an OEC is measurable 'in one to two weeks' is in the researcher's disagreement log but not in the fetched quote ('the duration of an experiment') - confirm in S2 before stating it; S13 has no outcome data for HEART (Google-internal examples on 20+ products); S12 is a 2016 record whose only case is Sears; S14 evaluates guideline applicability (49 practitioners, 20 AI products), not retention or revenue; the Amazon 'Type 1 / Type 2' labels are not on the fetched letter - use S15's 'two-way doors' wording or mark unverified; S17 and S1 do not mention OKRs on the fetched pages - report silence, not opposition. Illustrations from ML features are hypothetical and carry no invented figures.
topics: The overall evaluation criterion: measurable within the experiment's duration yet believed to causally drive long-term objectives; why profit is a poor OEC and customer lifetime value a strong one (S2 Ch. 1 pp. 6, 12)
Guardrail metrics as the statement of what the organization will not trade away; 'percent of plan delivered' as an anti-metric (S2 Ch. 1 pp. 12, 22)
Strategy drives the OEC and experiments hill-climb within it; the three organizational tenets that make experimentation work (S2 Ch. 1 pp. 11, 21)
PULSE vs HEART (Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success); per-user normalization of raw counts; why seven-day actives can rise under 100% weekly turnover (S13)

Goals-Signals-Metrics: how the process surfaces disagreement about goals; the Gmail five-or-more-days-per-week metric and its link to longer-term retention; metrics evaluate launched products and do not replace formative research (S13)
Experiment results as a portfolio: expect most work to be thrown away (Slack), most big redesigns fail, mostly near-optimization plus a few radical bets (S2 Ch. 1 Tenet 3, Scenario 2)
Twyman's law and trust in results: a figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong (S2 Preface)

Evidence vs judgment: data-driven as informing the HiPPO (S2); decide at about 70% of the information, disagree and commit, and resist proxies such as process and survey averages (S15); the Apple no-ad-test counterexample (S2); metrics tied to goals and triangulated (S13)
OKR mechanics: three to five objectives, about three key results each, 0.0-1.0 grading with a 0.6-0.7 sweet spot, annual and quarterly cadence, public, not performance reviews (S12)
Alignment alternatives and where each fails: one composite OEC with guardrails (S2), initiatives plus a product timeline (S17), appetite-bounded bets (S1)

Probabilistic features: why AI-infused systems violate classic usability heuristics (false positives and negatives); the 18 human-AI guidelines in four phases; G2 'how well it can do what it can do', G11 'why it did what it did', G14 'update and adapt cautiously' (S14)

Speed vs trust: 10,000+ experiments a year at Bing (S2) against change aversion (S13), 'update and adapt cautiously' (S14), 'iterate too much' (S18) and 'constant, erratic change' (S6); offline-vs-online evaluation of ML features is a stated gap (unverified)
disagreements: Evidence vs judgment: how much data before acting?
Aligning teams to goals: OKRs, a single OEC with guardrails, initiatives, or bets?
Speed of change vs user trust (relevant to ML features that adapt over time)

modules.title: Who Decides and What Carries the Decision: Product Roles and Spec Artifacts
modules.description: Who owns what in a product team - from CEO-of-the-product to engineer-led teams and the AI-era builder - and which document (PRD, prototype, pitch, PR/FAQ, short project spec) carries the decision to the people who build.
modules.scope: In: the role models found in the sources (PM as CEO of the product; PM with no authority; engineer-led teams with the PM as compass at PostHog; rotating engineer leads with one PM at Linear; the trio with split risk ownership; Shape Up's betting table that names no PM) with the decision rights and mechanisms of each; what a product-minded engineer does and what that earns; AI-era shifts in PM work; the spec artifacts - ten-step PRD, prototype as spec, pitch, PR/FAQ, one-to-two-page project spec - with structure, author, cost and the risk each de-risks. Out: the four risks themselves (page 1), prioritization (page 3), stakeholder conflict and viability (page 6), PM careers, hiring and levels (excluded), organizational transformation (excluded). After reading, the reader can say which decisions he owns or can claim as an engineer under each team model, what the PM is accountable for in each, and which artifact fits a given decision. Writer cautions: all structure evidence is self-reported by builder organizations (S18, S19, S20) and no source compares PM-led with engineer-led outcomes - say so; S21 was written about 15 years before its 2012 posting and its host warns it is probably not relevant to today's PMs - present it as the dated position it is; S24's Engineer:PM ratios (6:1, range 4:1-10:1) are Andrew Ng's unsourced assertion and the only source for them - attribute and mark unverified, never present as a finding, and omit the later lower ratios (secondary only); PostHog's split-at-six and '8+ products' are S19's self-report (S20 confirms the operating model, not the counts); S23 has no data and does not address infrastructure or platform teams - state this gap, it matters for an inference-runtime engineer; S8 (2005) and S6 (2026) are by the same author - present the change as one of primacy, not kind (S8 Step 5 already prototypes); S16's page gives no length limit for the press release and does not mention a six-page memo - do not state either; S27 is not used. As of 2026-10-26; AI-era claims (S6, S24) and PostHog's handbook are likely to change within a year.
topics: Position A, the PM as CEO of the product: defines the what and not the how, manages the product team, focuses it on revenue and customers; a Netscape-era memo (S21)
Position B, you are not the CEO: no direct authority over the functions that decide success, authority is earned, product management is a team sport; and the 2026 'builder, not a manager' (S22, S6)

Engineer-led at PostHog: engineers own sprint planning and spec'ing, PMs as the team's compass, one interview per week per PM, a monthly growth review for products with fit, teams that split at six, teams with no PM, and the founders' 'I was (partially) wrong' reversal (S19, S20)

Engineer-led at Linear: engineers lead projects on a rotating basis, one PM in the company, what counts as a project, weekly updates, engineers deciding readiness, and why the model leans on a small senior team (S18, S17)

The trio and risk ownership as a decision-rights map: PM for value and viability, designer for usability, lead engineer for feasibility; the PM's 'dozens or even hundreds of decisions every day' (S3, S9, S6)

The product-minded engineer: S23's behaviors - do not settle for the spec, understand the business and its data, offer trade-offs upfront, map edge cases and cut work on them, validate usage, own results - as concrete decision points; the career claim has no data (S23)
AI-era shifts: prototypes get cheaper, clear specs gain value, strong PMs prototype, engineers adopt AI faster than PMs; the Engineer:PM ratio as one unsourced figure (S24, S6)
The 2005 PRD: purpose, ten steps, prioritized and measurable objectives, and 'over-confidence in specs' as the commonest mistake (S8)
Prototype as spec (2026): the PRD kept for use cases and non-functional requirements, not a substitute for discovery (S6)
The pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes, no-gos, at deliberately low fidelity (S1 Ch. 6)
The PR/FAQ: working backwards from the customer announcement, a first draft in hours, external then internal FAQ, silent reading, about ten reviewers, the AWS case that took more than a year (S16)

Linear's one-to-two-page project spec for situational awareness with a named owner, and a decision table for choosing an artifact by what it carries, who writes it, its cost and the risk it de-risks (S17, S18)
disagreements: Who decides what gets built: the PM as CEO of the product, the engineer, or a cross-functional trio?
What is the right spec artifact: PRD, prototype, pitch, PR/FAQ, or a short project spec?

modules.title: Business Viability for a Developer Product: Stakeholders, Strategy, Pricing and Positioning
modules.description: The risk engineers underweight: how stakeholder constraints, strategic position, pricing and positioning decide whether a developer or infrastructure product works as a business, and exactly where the evidence stops.
modules.scope: In: business viability as the fourth risk and why it is the neglected one; stakeholders as suppliers of business constraints and what a product team must demonstrate to them; decision under disagreement (70% information, two-way doors, disagree and commit, process as proxy); four competing definitions of strategy; commoditizing complements; the pricing mechanics of a developer product from PostHog's published rules and Stripe's five models and their trade-offs; a half-section on positioning; the infrastructure/platform-team gap. Out: willingness-to-pay research, inference unit economics and COGS, go-to-market motions, opportunity sizing and business cases, strategy frameworks (Helmer, Porter), platform-product management, PM careers - all course candidates with no fetched source. After reading, the reader can name the viability questions a runtime or SDK product must answer, derive which price metric fits a stated cost structure, read PostHog's rules as one company's policy and not a consensus, and say which parts of the page are evidence and which are inference. This is the thinnest page in the plan: do not pad, and report back if 6,000 words cannot be reached from the sources without padding. Planned unverified marks (budget 8 per module): (1) applying usage-pricing logic to on-device inference, where the marginal compute runs on the customer's hardware - S26 itself covers AI coding tools, the application is the planner's inference; (2) Dunford's five positioning components - S31 is the author's book page and names none, the names exist only in secondary summaries; do not state a publication year, the edition is unresolved; (3) Rumelt's kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action) - S30 gives a table of contents and publisher copy, the kernel is attested only by search snippets, cite page numbers only as the Profile Books UK edition's; (4) mapping complements and substitutes onto an inference runtime versus hardware vendors and model providers - S25 is a verbal argument with no elasticity data; (5) stakeholder conflict resolution and handling executive demands - S7 gives no method and defers to a book; (6) which mechanisms transfer to internal platform teams - no source, S23 itself omits them, S27 is only a first-edition table-of-contents pointer ('Keys to Platform Products') and may not survive into the second edition; (7) any price, margin or licensing figure for an on-device runtime - none exists in the source map, never invent one. PostHog's rules (match the cheapest competitor with real revenue, no per-seat charge, a free tier that is a one-way door) are one company's policy (S20); S26 is a billing vendor's qualitative guidance with no prices, margins or churn data - do not repeat its '88% of businesses use AI' figure. S3 is the only source on what viability includes (go-to-market and sales-channel fit). S25 is a 2002 essay; date it. As of 2026-10-26; PostHog's policies and Stripe's guidance are likely to change within a year.
topics: Business viability risk: its definition, its inclusion of go-to-market and sales-channel fit, why it is the risk product managers and engineers under-estimate, and 'tackle value and business risk early' (S3)

Stakeholders as suppliers of business constraints: who counts as a stakeholder, sharing business context, reframing requests, direct access to customers and data, demonstrating that the team understands the constraints (S7)
Decision under disagreement: about 70% of the information, two-way doors, disagree and commit, process as a proxy for outcomes (S15); authority earned rather than conferred (S22)
What no fetched source supplies: a method for conflicting stakeholder constraints or executive demands (S7 defers to a book) - stated as a gap, with the unverified items marked

Four definitions of strategy: Rumelt's publisher claim that strategy is not ambition, vision or planning (kernel unverified), Cagan's vision plus prioritized objectives, Kohavi's strategy as the choice of OEC, Spolsky's positional economics (S30, S4, S2, S25)
Commoditize your complements: substitute vs complement, demand rises as complement prices fall, the IBM, Netscape and Sun/HP examples; a verbal argument with no elasticity figures (S25)
Applying complements to an inference runtime relative to hardware vendors, model providers and app developers: a derived mapping from S25's premises, marked unverified

PostHog's pricing rules as a mechanism: usage-based default, price tracks usage, flat fees only where cost does not scale, match the cheapest competitor making real revenue, no per-seat charge, paid-plan default for new features, free tier as a one-way door, enterprise gating, yearly review, admitted uncertainty about cost base (S20)

Stripe's five models and their trade-offs: per-seat (simple, cross-subsidy), tiered, capability-based (needs obvious differentiation), usage-based (unpredictability slows adoption), hybrid; flat seats plus heavy agentic usage create a margin problem; mistakes show after about 12 months (S26)

Choosing a price metric from the cost structure and the value structure: a symbolic derived framework from S20 and S26, with the on-device inversion (marginal compute on the customer's device) marked unverified and no price figures
Positioning as a half-section: what the author's book page claims (five components, three styles, market trends); component names unverified (S31)
The infrastructure and platform gap and where the evidence ends: S23's own omission, S27's table-of-contents pointer, and the list of areas that need a course
disagreements: Pricing a developer or infrastructure product
What a strategy is and where product strategy comes from
